units.title: Ethereum mainnet reference and cross-chain deployment parity

code.title: hook and native sides
code.task: The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/v4math.py is a transcription of the math libraries, research/network-risk/opcodes/jumpmap.json maps every conditional jump of the build to its source line, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with sections on what cycles 10 to 25 added and a list of what is not covered. Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Do not install software. Python 3, rustc 1.97 with cargo, go 1.24, node and the system C and C++ compilers are present, and you may compile downloaded source inside your own work directory. Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. Do not download compiler toolchains or other binaries to run them; source archives are fine. Record every sampling seed, save every mismatch record in full, and bracket each batch of calls to a public endpoint with web3_clientVersion so the build that answered is known. If an endpoint refuses your client (HTTP 403, 429 or a challenge page), record that and use another public endpoint; do not try to get around the refusal and use no API keys. Analysis only: no exploit code and no transactions. Lead L-1103. Cycle 25 ran 1,533 cases through one eth_call with state overrides at the real PoolManager address of all 21 networks (research/network-risk/cycles/025/theme-unexecuted-sides.work: the driver, the case list, out/ and the exact-fraction checker of its Task 3) and covered 88 of the 117 branch sides that no producer of MegaETH, Monad or HyperEVM has executed. Every case used a hookless pool and ERC-20 token doubles. Four sides were left out: the hook return delta at src/PoolManager.sol:181, a hook that changes the amount to swap at src/libraries/Pool.sol:320 (through beforeSwap's delta in src/libraries/Hooks.sol:250-290), a native settle with value while an ERC-20 is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:356), and native value paths in general (settle with msg.value at :353-354, native take through CALL at src/types/Currency.sol:45-49, a take to an address that rejects value). The hook call path is where the PoolManager depends most on CALL semantics: the gas forwarded, RETURNDATASIZE and RETURNDATACOPY of the callee's answer (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:126-150), the selector check on the returned word, the parse of a returned int256 into two int128 halves (src/types/BeforeSwapDelta.sol, src/types/BalanceDelta.sol), the dynamic fee override with its flag bit (src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol), and the address bits that decide which hook functions are called (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:27-45). Task 1: extend the cycle 25 driver, compiled with the solc-js 0.8.26 already used for research/network-risk/build, with a hook double placed by state override at addresses whose low 14 bits enable each permission in turn and in the combinations that the address validation at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:86-120 accepts. The hook double returns, per case, a chosen selector and chosen delta words. Cover: every hook function called with a correct selector and with a wrong one; beforeSwap returning a specified delta that reduces the amount to zero, flips its sign (expect the revert at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:268-275), or leaves a remainder of 1; beforeSwap returning a dynamic fee override with and without the flag bit and with a fee above 1,000,000; afterSwap, afterAddLiquidity and afterRemoveLiquidity returning deltas in both currencies, at the int128 bounds, and with the return-delta permission bit off; a hook that returns fewer than 32 bytes, more than expected, or reverts with empty, short and long data (src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol bubbleUpAndRevertWith); a hook that calls back into the PoolManager (swap, modifyLiquidity, donate, sync, take, settle, mint, burn, a second unlock) from inside each hook function; a hook that consumes all gas but 1/64. Task 2: native value. With a balance override on the caller, cover settle with value in a native pool, settle with value while an ERC-20 is synced (expect NonzeroNativeValue), sync of the native currency after an ERC-20 sync, settle with zero value, take of native to an account without code, to a contract that reverts on value, to a precompile address (0x01 to 0x0a, and each network's own precompile and system addresses listed in research/network-risk/networks.json or the network profiles), to the PoolManager itself and to address zero, and native settleFor. On Celo, Polygon, Arc and Tempo the native asset also has a contract face or does not exist as value at all; run the same cases there and say what each returns. Task 3: run every case on all 21 networks, bracketed by web3_clientVersion, and compare each returned word with the Ethereum answer and with pyevm.py. On Monad also run the PoolManager frames through the compiled harness of cycle 23 with one world per case. Record which jumpmap sides each case executes with pyevm_cov.py (research/network-risk/cycles/025/theme-unexecuted-sides.work has the copy used) and list the sides of the 387 that are still not run by any case of cycles 24 to 26. Task 4: check the results against rules that do not come from src/: after every unlock the sum of what callers paid equals the rise of the PoolManager's balances less what it paid out, per currency; a hook can take at most what the swapper's delta loses; no case ends with a nonzero delta count and a successful unlock; a failed hook call leaves no state behind. Report every case that breaks a rule, with the words, even if all networks agree with each other.

code.title: monad shipped binary
code.task: The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/v4math.py is a transcription of the math libraries, research/network-risk/opcodes/jumpmap.json maps every conditional jump of the build to its source line, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with sections on what cycles 10 to 25 added and a list of what is not covered. Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Do not install software. Python 3, rustc 1.97 with cargo, go 1.24, node and the system C and C++ compilers are present, and you may compile downloaded source inside your own work directory. Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. Do not download compiler toolchains or other binaries to run them; source archives are fine. Record every sampling seed, save every mismatch record in full, and bracket each batch of calls to a public endpoint with web3_clientVersion so the build that answered is known. If an endpoint refuses your client (HTTP 403, 429 or a challenge page), record that and use another public endpoint; do not try to get around the refusal and use no API keys. Analysis only: no exploit code and no transactions. Leads L-1104 and L-1108. Monad runs the hot PoolManager as native x86 code in blocks, eth_call and trace calls on its public endpoints use the interpreter (finding F-130), and every result on the compiled path so far comes from a harness built locally from source at v0.16.5 and v0.16.7 (research/network-risk/cycles/023/theme-monad-compiled-coverage.work, src/harness.cpp). Nobody has checked that the binaries validators run contain the same emitter, the same asmjit and the same build options as that local build. Cycle 25 also saw two effects in the harness and put them down to the harness without reading the code: the interpreter side gave different results between runs of one scenario when one world held about 3,000 token accounts (research/network-risk/cycles/025/theme-unexecuted-sides.work/out/hx/rep1369.txt against rep1369b.txt), and the native result of case 1528 differs only on the first scenario of a process. Task 1: find how Monad distributes validator binaries for mainnet (the release page names v0.16.5 for mainnet and v0.16.7 for testnet and RPC; packages come from an apt repository or a container registry named in Monad's node operator documentation). If a package can be fetched without credentials, download it into dl/ and inspect it without executing any file from it: use only tools already present (ar, tar, readelf, objdump, strings, nm, Python). Record package name, version, hash, the compiler and flags the binary names (.comment section, build id, -march, LTO traces), which asmjit version strings it carries, and the CPU features it requires or selects at run time. If no package can be fetched, say what was tried and what refused, and do the same reading from the published Dockerfiles, CMake presets and CI files of the tagged source. Task 2: compare with the harness build. Locate in the shipped binary the emitter functions for SHL, SHR and SAR by a non-literal shift, MUL, MULMOD, ADDMOD, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, EXP, SIGNEXTEND, BYTE, the comparisons, JUMPI and the memory expansion check, by symbol if symbols exist, otherwise by string references, constants and call structure. Disassemble them and the same functions of the harness object code, and state for each whether the instruction sequences are equal, equal up to register allocation and layout, or different. For every difference say whether it can change a result word. Compare the runtime routines the emitted code calls (the uint256 library: mulmod, addmod, udivrem, exp, signextend, sar) the same way. Task 3: read src/harness.cpp and the Monad VM code it links (the varcode cache, the compiler's code cache, the host and state interface). Find the cause of both harness effects named above: is each a property of the harness host (account map, storage callbacks, the virtual router at harness.cpp:421-423) or of Monad code (a cache keyed on something that process history changes, uninitialised memory, a data race between the asynchronous compiler thread and the executing thread)? If the cause is in Monad code, say whether a validator can hit it and what a block would then contain. Rerun the two scenarios with the cause removed or controlled and report the results. Say which earlier harness runs used a shared large world and whether they need a rerun; rerun them if so. Task 4: Monad compiles a contract asynchronously once the interpreter gas spent on it passes a threshold, so two validators can run the same call one interpreted and one compiled. List every place where the two paths could give different observable results by design or by a known issue: gas accounting at block boundaries of the compiled code, out-of-gas position, memory expansion, stack overflow and underflow checks, the depth limit, and exceptional halts in the middle of a basic block. For the PoolManager bytecode, give the basic blocks in which an out-of-gas or a stack check is moved to the block start, and say whether any PoolManager state or outgoing call can differ between the two paths when a call runs out of gas inside such a block.

code.title: stateful interpreter
code.task: The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/v4math.py is a transcription of the math libraries, research/network-risk/opcodes/jumpmap.json maps every conditional jump of the build to its source line, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with sections on what cycles 10 to 25 added and a list of what is not covered. Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Do not install software. Python 3, rustc 1.97 with cargo, go 1.24, node and the system C and C++ compilers are present, and you may compile downloaded source inside your own work directory. Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. Do not download compiler toolchains or other binaries to run them; source archives are fine. Record every sampling seed, save every mismatch record in full, and bracket each batch of calls to a public endpoint with web3_clientVersion so the build that answered is known. If an endpoint refuses your client (HTTP 403, 429 or a challenge page), record that and use another public endpoint; do not try to get around the refusal and use no API keys. Analysis only: no exploit code and no transactions. Lead L-1115, widened to all networks. The opcode battery runs each vector in a fresh frame, and the script sets run short sequences. Several clients now keep state inside the interpreter between instructions, frames or transactions: bor keeps a memo of MULMOD reciprocals per EVM (core/vm/mulmod_memo.go, read at v2.12.0-beta), erigon 3.8 keeps a storage read cache per frame (finding F-147), reth and revm keep analysed bytecode and jump tables in caches keyed by code hash, Monad keeps a varcode cache and compiled code per contract, MegaETH keeps SALT buckets and resource counters, Nitro keeps a per-block cache of recent WASM and of transient storage, and geth-derived clients keep per-transaction access lists, refund counters and a transient storage journal. A stale entry in one of these would give a wrong word only after a particular history, which is a shape an ordinary account can line up through its own pools in one long transaction. Task 1: for each client behind the 21 networks (builds as recorded in research/network-risk/OPCODES.md and the newest network profiles), list every piece of interpreter state that outlives one instruction: what it is keyed by, when an entry is written, when it is invalidated, and whether it can outlive a revert of the frame that wrote it, a SELFDESTRUCT, a CREATE2 that redeploys different code at one address in the same transaction, or the end of the transaction. Give file and line. Name each case where the key is narrower than the input (a truncated modulus, a code hash without the chain's spec id, an address without the storage incarnation). Task 2: build long sequences that run inside one eth_call with state overrides at the real PoolManager address, with this checkout's build (the cycle 25 driver in research/network-risk/cycles/025/theme-unexecuted-sides.work can be extended): (a) 64 and 512 consecutive swaps across 16 pools whose liquidity values give distinct, repeated and alternating denominators in FullMath.mulDiv (src/libraries/FullMath.sol:24-48) and in mulDivRoundingUp, including denominators that differ only in their top or bottom 64 bits, in both swap directions; (b) the same swap repeated before and after a reverted inner call that used a different denominator; (c) reads of one pool slot through extsload before a write, after a write, after a reverted write and after a write in a nested unlock callback of a hook; (d) transient storage written, read through exttload, reverted in an inner frame and read again, across 300 currencies in one unlock; (e) a hook address whose code is replaced in the same call by a CREATE2 redeploy after SELFDESTRUCT where the network still allows it, then called again. Run each on all 21 networks, bracketed by web3_clientVersion, and compare every returned word with Ethereum and with pyevm.py. On Polygon run them against each bor build the public endpoints report and say which build answered. On Monad run the PoolManager frames through the compiled harness as well. Task 3: eth_call does not carry state between transactions. For the caches that outlive a transaction (analysed code, compiled code, bor's memo if it is per EVM instance, erigon's cache if it is per block), find mined blocks on Polygon, Monad, Base, Tempo and Ethereum in which several PoolManager transactions follow each other with different denominators or with a write to a slot that a later transaction reads, and compare traced results with the committed state (the cycle 23 committed.py and cycle 25 research/network-risk/cycles/025/theme-speculative-commit.work scripts). Give the number of blocks, words and every mismatch. Task 4: for bor, read the MULMOD memo at the newest tagged release and at any tag that carries the Salvador fork (block 98,688,600, 8 December 2026). State the exact condition under which a memo entry is reused, prove from the code that a reused reciprocal belongs to the same full 256-bit modulus, and test the memo function directly from source, compiled inside the work directory with the go toolchain present, on at least one million pairs of moduli that share their top or bottom limbs.

code.title: deferred verification
code.task: The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/v4math.py is a transcription of the math libraries, research/network-risk/opcodes/jumpmap.json maps every conditional jump of the build to its source line, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with sections on what cycles 10 to 25 added and a list of what is not covered. Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Do not install software. Python 3, rustc 1.97 with cargo, go 1.24, node and the system C and C++ compilers are present, and you may compile downloaded source inside your own work directory. Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. Do not download compiler toolchains or other binaries to run them; source archives are fine. Record every sampling seed, save every mismatch record in full, and bracket each batch of calls to a public endpoint with web3_clientVersion so the build that answered is known. If an endpoint refuses your client (HTTP 403, 429 or a challenge page), record that and use another public endpoint; do not try to get around the refusal and use no API keys. Analysis only: no exploit code and no transactions. Leads L-1106, L-1111, L-1100 and L-1110. Three of the 21 networks have moved, or are moving, the point at which a block's execution is checked. Avalanche accepts a block before executing it (cycle 25, research/network-risk/cycles/025/theme-avalanche-sae.research.json, finding F-152). Tempo's T14 fork on 8 December 2026 brings deferred verification, under which a block can be notarized before its execution result is verified, and Tempo has one client. Monad executes after consensus by design. Arc's node separates consensus and execution over an RPC transport that v0.9.0 announces it will remove, and Arc runs unpublished commits. The question for the PoolManager is narrow: can a state that a user's wallet, a router or a bridge reads at the newest block (a balance, a pool price, a receipt for a take) belong to a block that is later replaced or whose execution result differs, and can an ordinary account cause or exploit that. Task 1, Tempo: read the T14 specification and the tempo release that carries it (v1.19.0 and v1.19.1, commit a9d6748). What exactly is deferred: which checks does a validator make before it votes, which after, and what happens to a notarized block whose execution turns out wrong (is it finalized anyway, is the chain halted, is the proposer slashed)? Which validators run binaries built with the jit feature (bin/tempo/Cargo.toml lines 267-268), by release notes, operator pages or build files; if any does, transcribe the LLVM stage rules for MULMOD, ADDMOD, SAR, SHL, SIGNEXTEND and JUMPI from evm2 and compare them with the specification. Lead L-1100: with --builder.parallel or the T15 candidate test is_payment_v3 (crates/payload/builder/src/prewarming.rs line 500), can a replayed action reach a contract other than a TIP-20 token or the channel reserve, for example a TIP-20 transfer whose recipient is the PoolManager followed by settle in the next transaction? Task 2, Monad: which block do eth_call, eth_getBalance and eth_getTransactionReceipt answer for at latest, safe and finalized on rpc.monad.xyz (read the RPC source at v0.16.7 and probe the endpoint with block tags, bracketed by web3_clientVersion)? Is latest a proposed block that can still be dropped, how often does a block served at latest not finalize (sample 2,000 heads and check them again after finality), and can a receipt for a PoolManager take served at latest belong to a block that never finalizes? Task 3, Arc: read the consensus to execution interface in the public arc-node branch and in what v0.9.0 announces. Does consensus vote on a block before the execution result is checked, and what does each block tag resolve to on rpc.mainnet.arc.io and arc.drpc.org? Task 4, the other networks in one table: for each of the 21, what latest, safe and finalized resolve to on the public endpoint, how far apart they are in blocks and seconds today, and who can replace a block served at latest (nobody, the sequencer, a proposer, an L1 reorganisation). Mark the networks where an ordinary account can make a block served at latest disappear. Task 5: read src/ for anything in the PoolManager whose safety depends on finality: none is expected, because every action settles inside one transaction; confirm or refute with file and line, including the ERC-6909 claims and the protocol fee accrual.
